newsitem.title: USA: Sorrow grips tornado-stricken town in Texas.
newsitem.headline: Sorrow grips tornado-stricken town in Texas.

text.p: Sorrow gripped this small Texas town on Thursday after officials began notifying families that their missing relatives were among the 27 people killed by a deadly tornado.

In a high school shelter for those who lost their homes in the storm that ripped through Jarrell on Tuesday, hope turned to tears as word came down late on Wednesday that remains found in the twisted wreckage had been identified as loved ones.
Young girls clutching teddy bears given them by rescue workers wept and hugged while adults tried to comfort them with pats on the back.
About 60 Jarrell residents went to the town football field where they sat in a circle, held hands and silently prayed as the sun set behind the nearby hills.
Families of the dead were led one by one into the white- frame First Baptist Church of Jarrell where local officials informed them of their loss.
"As you can imagine, there's a lot of anxiety and a lot of pain at the church right now," said Sherri Deatherage Green, a spokeswoman for the Texas Department of Public Safety.
She said the notification process, delayed until Wednesday night by the difficulty in identifying the mangled bodies of the tornado victims, would go on long into the night.

The identities of only four of the dead were made public, pending the notification of all the families. They included a five-year-old boy, a 44-year-old woman, and two school-age brothers, Deatherage Green said.

The delay had fostered hope among many here that their missing relatives had somehow survived when the tornado swept down a small valley on the outskirts of Jarrell, a town of 600 people 40 miles (64 km) north of Austin, Texas, and destroyed 50 homes. Adding to the uncertainty was a list of 23 people that police said were unaccounted for, but not confirmed dead.

An exhaustive search of the 4-mile-long (6.4 km) path of destruction left by the twister turned up no more victims than the 27 dead found immediately after the storm, officials said on Wednesday. They were to meet early on Thursday to determine whether the search should continue.
Deatherage Green said officials were uncertain whether there were 23 people missing or any at all.
"That's really an unknown number at this point," she told reporters. "It could be anything at this point."

Max Johnson, pastor of the First Baptist Church, said the town's grieving process could now finally begin. "It has been kind of frustrating because of all the unknowns...it's like a thorn in your foot you need to pull out," he said.
He said the dead were thought to include a family of five, all members of his church choir, who were trapped in their home when the giant tornado struck.

"It's a terrible thing, but I believe that no matter what happens, there's some good that come out of it," he said. In this case, Johnson said, the good was subtle: "It kind of reminds us of how temporary we are."
